Arguments from the sequential-decision setting\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/s11238-009-9145-3\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2009, 5, 5]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1016/0021-9045(80)90084-2\", \"title\": [\"The convergence and continuity of rational functions closely related to Padé approximants\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1016/0021-9045(80)90084-2\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[1980, 2]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.6150626\", \"title\": [\"The Elimination Cascade: Why Instrumental Convergence May Favor Preservation Over Elimination\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The instrumental convergence thesis holds that sufficiently intelligent agents will converge on goals like resource acquisition and obstacle removal regardless of terminal objectives. This paper presents a countervailing argument: for agents with complex, human-derived goals, elimination strategies are self-undermining. We formalize this via dependency graphs, showing that entities not immediately necessary for a goal may be transitively necessary through indirect chains. An agent following an elimination strategy will, in environments with sufficient dependency depth, destroy the conditions for its own goal-satisfaction. We prove that under uncertainty about dependency structure, combined with irreversibility of elimination and asymmetric error costs, rational agents should adopt preservation rather than elimination strategies-even superintelligent ones. The argument applies most strongly to goals that are complex, open-ended, or semantically dependent on human interpretive communities, precisely the class of goals most likely to emerge from training on human data. We connect this result to a game-theoretic model of AGI-human cooperation, showing that the elimination cascade argument and cooperation stability conditions are mutually reinforcing.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6150626\", \"published\": {\"date-p…

We connect this result to a game-theoretic model of AGI-human cooperation, showing that the elimination cascade argument and cooperation stability conditions are mutually reinforcing.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6150626\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/s11238-020-09772-2\", \"title\": [\"A theory of instrumental and existential rational decisions: Smith, Weber, Mauss, Tönnies after Martin Buber\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>This paper proffers a dialogical theory of decision-making: decision-makers (DMs) are engaged in two modes of rational decisions, instrumental and existential.
